sections.skill: Choose a test whose expected result would reveal a defect

questions.prompt: What does a test compare?

choices.text: The code's speed with the internet speed
The code's length with the length of another program
The code's result with an expected result you worked out

questions.correct_answer: The code's result with an expected result you worked out
questions.intro: A TEST runs code on a chosen input and compares the result with the EXPECTED result you worked out yourself. A good test is one that would FAIL if a particular mistake were present. To catch a mistake at a limit, test the limit itself. Example: the rule is "18 or older is an adult." A function using "age > 18" looks right and gives True for 20, but it wrongly gives False for 18. Only a test with age 18 reveals this. Choose tests by asking: "What mistake might be here, and which input would expose it?"

sections.skill: Pick the input that exposes a suspected mistake

questions.prompt: Which input exposes > 50 versus >= 50?
questions.intro: Work backward from the mistake. Ask: "If the code had this mistake, which input would give a different answer from the correct code?" Example: a free-shipping rule says "orders of 50 dollars or more ship free." Suspected mistake: using > 50 instead of >= 50. Inputs 30 and 80 give the same answers either way. Only input 50 differs: the correct rule says free, the mistaken one says not free. So 50 is the test to run, expecting "free."

questions.prompt: A test's expected answer was copied from the code's output. What is the problem?

choices.text: It only checks the code agrees with itself
Nothing, because the code's own output is always the most reliable expected answer

questions.correct_answer: It only checks the code agrees with itself
questions.intro: Tests can be weak in several ways. A test whose expected answer was copied from the code's own output only checks that the code agrees with itself. A test that uses only typical inputs may never reach the buggy part. And a test that checks too little, such as "the result is a number," passes even when the number is wrong. Strong tests use expected answers worked out independently and target the boundaries and special cases.

questions.prompt: A test checks only that the result "is a number." Why is it weak?

choices.text: It passes even when the number is wrong
Because numbers can never be checked by tests
